title: Infinitely Many Primes ≡ 1 (mod 4)
description: Proves there are infinitely many primes congruent to 1 modulo 4 using an elementary argument based on Fermat's theorem on sums of two squares. Considers N = (2·(n+1)!)² + 1 and shows every odd prime factor p of N satisfies p ≡ 1 (mod 4), since -1 is a square mod p (Euler's criterion). Uses Mathlib's Nat.Prime.mod_four_ne_three_of_dvd_isSquare_neg_one. 5 theorems, 0 definitions, 0 axioms.

overview.historicalContext: The infinitude of primes ≡ 1 (mod 4) is more subtle than the ≡ 3 case. The standard elementary argument uses the fact that if p | k² + 1, then -1 is a square mod p, hence p ≡ 1 (mod 4) by Euler's criterion. This was known to Euler and uses the theory of quadratic residues, in contrast to the purely congruential argument for p ≡ 3 (mod 4).
overview.problemStatement: Prove that for every n : ℕ, there exists a prime p > n with p ≡ 1 (mod 4), using N = (2·(n+1)!)² + 1 and Euler's criterion for quadratic residues.
overview.text: The key lemma prime_dvd_sq_add_one_mod_four: if odd prime p divides k² + 1, then p ≡ 1 (mod 4). Proof: k² ≡ -1 (mod p) means -1 is a square in ZMod p, which Mathlib's mod_four_ne_three_of_dvd_isSquare_neg_one converts to p ≢ 3 (mod 4); since p is an odd prime, p ≡ 1 (mod 4). For the main theorem: N = (2·(n+1)!)² + 1 is odd (even² + 1) and > 1, so has an odd prime factor p. p cannot equal 2 (N is odd). By the key lemma p ≡ 1 (mod 4). If p ≤ n then p | (n+1)!, so p | N - (2·(n+1)!)² = 1, contradicting primality.
overview.proofStrategy: prime_dvd_sq_add_one_mod_four: construct IsSquare (-1 : ZMod p) using k as witness from k² + 1 ≡ 0, then apply Mathlib's lemma. Main: contradiction for p ≤ n via Nat.dvd_factorial + Nat.Prime.not_dvd_one. Set-infinite formulation via Set.infinite_iff_exists_gt.
keyInsights: N = (2·(n+1)!)² + 1 is the p ≡ 1 analogue of 4·(n+1)!-1 used for p ≡ 3
-1 is a square mod p iff p ≡ 1 (mod 4): Euler's criterion is the key bridge
The argument requires quadratic residues; the p ≡ 3 case only needed products mod 4
Compare: for p ≡ 3, multiply-mod-4 suffices; for p ≡ 1, we need -1 square mod p
prerequisites: Euler's criterion: -1 is a square mod p iff p ≡ 1 (mod 4)

conclusion.summary: Infinitely many primes ≡ 1 (mod 4) via N = (2·(n+1)!)² + 1 and Euler's criterion. Uses Mathlib's isSquare_neg_one lemma. 5 theorems, 0 axioms, 177 lines.
conclusion.implications: The contrast between the proofs for p ≡ 1 and p ≡ 3 illustrates the increasing complexity of Euclid-style arguments as one descends into quadratic residue theory. Together they formalize infinitude for all non-trivial residue classes mod 4.
